Inaugural Armadillo Ball at Stable Hall brings together Rattlesnake Milk, dancing and fun

Even though this was the Lone Star Beer-sponsored festival’s first installment, it felt like it’s always been here.
by Stephanie Koithan November 22, 2026November 22, 2026

Share this:

  • Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email
  • Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit
  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
  • Share on Nextdoor (Opens in new window) Nextdoor
  • Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky

San Antonio, a city steeped in tradition, just got a new one.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:08
Instaread

Lone Star Beer held its inaugural Armadillo Ball at Pearl’s Stable Hall Friday night. Even though it was the event’s debut, the festival was so well curated and perfectly suited to the space that it felt like it had always been there.

The Armadillo Ball brought together live music, dancing and a vendor market with shopping and activations around the room, including tintype photographs by Holliday Tin Type, chainstitch embroidery by Lunchroom Anxiety, high-end men’s Western wear by Richter Goods and items from other local businesses.

The evening opened with tunes curated by DJ acts Strawberry Jams and Viaje, who mixed old-school selections with country classics.

Rattlesnake Milk, a band from the Texas Panhandle, was the headliner of the evening. Known for conjuring a sense of prairieland desolation in their sound, it’s only a matter of time before the act lands on a soundtrack and blow the fuck up.

We’re just lucky they’re ours — for now.

Drawing comparisons to the desert soundscapes of Hermanos Gutiérrez, the band adds a coyote yip for good measure in the yodeling vocals of singer-songwriter Lou Lewis.

Lewis began writing and recording early demos while farming cotton near Olton, later forming the band around 2012 with friends in the Lubbock area.

These days, Rattlesnake Milk regularly sell out Texas venues, as they did during recent performances at Gruene Hall, the Lonesome Rose and Friday night’s show at Stable Hall. They’ve also played iconic venues like Red Rocks Amphitheatre, opening for Charley Crockett.

The group’s sound appeals to both alt-country purists and more casual fans who mostly listen to pop, judging by the looks of the crowds they draw.

At Stable Hall, they played some of their most beloved and intoxicating tracks, such as “.38 Special,” “Holy Ghost” and “Cowboy Killers.” But they also opened the set with several new tracks from an as-yet-untitled album, guitarist Andrew Chavez told the Current.

“It’s funny, we spent so many years spending money on Lone Stars, and now they’re paying us,” Lewis told the audience.

Photographs by Oscar Moreno.
